positioning: The cat that looks like a tiny mountain lion. Ancient, athletic, and endlessly busy.
story: The Abyssinian looks like it stepped off the wall of an Egyptian tomb, and that resemblance helped build its legend. It is one of the oldest breeds in the fancy. Its true origins likely lie around the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia, but it took its name from Abyssinia, modern Ethiopia, where early show cats were said to come from.

The signature is the coat. Each hair is banded with several colors, a pattern called ticking, which gives the warm ruddy coat a glowing, wild-rabbit shimmer that shifts as the cat moves. The lithe body, large ears, and almond eyes complete the look of a miniature cougar.

Abyssinians are pure motion. They are athletic, curious, and busy, forever climbing to the highest shelf, opening cupboards, and supervising every task in the house. Owners call them the clowns of the cat world, and a bored Aby will invent its own entertainment.

For all that energy they are deeply people-oriented, less of a lap cat and more of a constant companion that wants to be in the room and in the action. CFA recognized the breed in 1906, and it has been a beloved fixture of the fancy ever since.

An Abyssinian needs a job, or it will appoint itself one. It is among the most active and clever of breeds, forever climbing, exploring, and helping with whatever you are doing, and it does best with tall perches, puzzle toys, and ideally a feline companion to match its energy.

The short coat is wash-and-wear, needing only an occasional brush, but the breed carries a few watch-points. Responsible breeders test for a blood disorder called PK deficiency, for an inherited eye condition, and for dental disease, all of which can run in the line. A fit, lean Aby tends to stay sprightly into old age.
fblocks: Named for Abyssinia, the old name for Ethiopia, where the first show cats were reported, though its real roots lie farther east.
Its build and ticked coat echo the cats of ancient Egyptian art, which fed its romantic origin story.
High-energy and clever, the Aby needs climbing space, toys, and company. It is interactive rather than a lap cat and dislikes being idle.
A short, close coat in which each hair is banded, giving a warm ticked shimmer, classically in ruddy and other warm tones.
Recognized by CFA in 1906 and one of the oldest breeds in the registry.
Give it height, puzzles, and company. The Aby is an athletic busybody that grows restless and loud when bored.
Easy to groom, but ask breeders about screening for the blood disorder PK deficiency and for eye and dental issues.
days: Abyssinian hairs are banded with several colors. That pattern is called ticking.
Named for Abyssinia, though the breed's roots may lie nearer the Indian Ocean.
An Aby can reach the top shelf before you finish saying its name.
Everything high is a perch and everything closed is a puzzle. The Aby is thorough.
A busy mind needs a tall place to think. Give it a shelf and some books.
Ask who supervised the dinner, the laundry, and the mail. The Aby was there.
Even a clown naps. A warm cushion on a low shelf is a small peace.
last_walk:
Lamplight on the stairs, and the house is finally still.
The Abyssinian has climbed, leapt, and checked every cupboard this week. Now it pauses on the bottom step, ears up, listening to the snow against the glass. One more look around, then bed.
